title: Benchmark report methodology (working draft) — latency per dollar
content:
Doc purpose
This is a working methodology draft for the public-facing benchmark report. It is explicitly incomplete and includes unresolved questions (flagged as OPEN QUESTION / TODO). The final version will live in Confluence (source of truth) and will be summarized on the public landing page.

Owners + review
- Methodology/design: Claire Dubois, Jonas Weber
- Harness + runner: Rina Kobayashi
- Metric normalization ($ + latency/$): Nadia Rahman
- Data validation + aggregation: Mei Lin
- Docs narrative: Elliot Price
- PMM/legal review pass (claims language): Soojin Lee + Michael Grant/Sofia Mendes (later)

Goals / non-goals
Goals
- Provide a reproducible, technically defensible description of how we measured and how to interpret results.
- Prevent “cherry-picking” perceptions by making workload definitions, runtime configuration, and inclusion/exclusion criteria explicit.
- Define how latency/$ is computed, with supporting metrics (p50/p95, throughput, $/1M tokens).

Non-goals
- Prove absolute “best” for every workload; results represent specific production-oriented mixes.
- Compare every competitor endpoint 1:1 (we may include contextual baselines with clear caveats).

Summary of what we are measuring
We report latency and cost efficiency for LLM inference across a curated set of models and regions on Redwood Inference.
Primary headline metric: latency per dollar (latency/$)
Supporting metrics:
- Time to first token (TTFT)
- Time per output token (TPOT) / decode latency
- End-to-end latency (request start to final token)
- Throughput (tokens/sec) at specified concurrency levels
- Cost ($/1M tokens) separated by input/output tokens where applicable

IMPORTANT: latency/$ is intended as a unit-economics-friendly metric that captures tradeoffs across both latency and spend. It is not the same as raw throughput.

Definitions (draft)
Request structure
Each request i has:
- input_tokens_i
- output_tokens_i (capped by max_output_tokens; actual output_tokens_i can be lower)
- start_time_i
- first_token_time_i
- end_time_i

Latency metrics
- TTFT_i = first_token_time_i - start_time_i
- E2E_i = end_time_i - start_time_i
- Decode_time_i = end_time_i - first_token_time_i
- TPOT_i = Decode_time_i / max(output_tokens_i, 1)

Aggregation (for a set of requests S)
- p50 / p95 computed across per-request TTFT and E2E distributions
- TPOT aggregated across per-request TPOT (not by dividing aggregate decode time by aggregate tokens)

Cost metrics
- $/1M tokens computed from metered usage * published price schedule for the deployment mode used in the benchmark (Hosted API baseline).
- We will publish the exact price schedule date and region pricing assumptions used.

Latency per dollar (proposed)
We want a single number per {model, region, workload, concurrency}.
Current implementation in benchmark-lab (see PR-4821) computes latency/$ as:
- latency_per_dollar = p50_E2E_ms / cost_per_request_usd
Where:
- cost_per_request_usd = (input_tokens * price_per_input_token + output_tokens * price_per_output_token)

OPEN QUESTION: Should headline latency/$ use p50_E2E, p95_E2E, or a blended score? Marketing prefers a simple “typical user experience” metric (p50), but buyers frequently care about p95 for production SLOs.
Proposed approach:
- Headline: latency/$ (p50 E2E)
- Always show p95 E2E in table + note that high variance / tail latency impacts user experience.

Workloads (draft)
We will benchmark multiple workloads because prefill vs decode characteristics differ strongly by application.
Each workload definition includes:
- prompt set (distribution of input lengths + task types)
- output token distribution or max_output_tokens
- concurrency level(s)
- sampling params (temperature, top_p, etc.)
- caching/batching configuration

Workload candidates (as of 6/19)
W1: “Production mix v3” (default)
- Prompt set: prompt-set-v3-production-mix (PR-4840)
- Composition (approx, subject to final):
  - 40% short chat turns (prefill 150–400 tokens, decode 80–200 tokens)
  - 35% support/agentic style (prefill 400–1,200 tokens, decode 150–400 tokens)
  - 15% long-context summarization (prefill 2,000–8,000 tokens, decode 200–600 tokens)
  - 10% tool/structured output (prefill 300–900 tokens, decode 50–150 tokens)

W2: Prefill-heavy
- Emphasize longer prompts / retrieval-augmented style
- Useful for “large context” positioning

W3: Decode-heavy
- Emphasize longer generations (copywriting, code generation)

OPEN QUESTION: Do we publish only W1 for launch (simpler), or include W2/W3 as optional tabs? Risk: more surface area increases “methodology argument” load and review time.

Prompt sets
- Prompt sets are versioned.
- We will provide:
  - prompt_set_version
  - high-level description of task categories
  - token length distributions (binned histograms)
  - a reproducibility package for internal reruns

Constraints
- Public artifacts must not contain customer text or sensitive prompts.
- Prompts are synthetic or licensed internal evaluation prompts.

Token distributions (draft plan)
We will publish binned distributions (not raw text) for:
- Input tokens: bins [0–256], [256–512], [512–1k], [1k–2k], [2k–4k], [4k–8k], [8k+]
- Output tokens: bins [0–64], [64–128], [128–256], [256–512], [512–1k], [1k+]

OPEN QUESTION: Where do we cap max input tokens for long-context in the public report? (Depends on model context windows and fairness across models.)
Proposed: include a “context length” filter on the interactive page with separate “<=2k” and “<=8k” views.

Models
We will publish a curated list of Redwood-supported open models (exact list to be finalized by Product + Applied ML).
For each model, publish:
- model identifier + revision hash (or Redwood model version)
- context window used
- quantization profile (if any)
- runtime engine version

OPEN QUESTION: Do we allow per-model quantization differences? If we do, we must disclose clearly and ensure quality guardrails.
Current direction: publish Redwood “recommended production profile” per model, but disclose profile details (e.g., fp16/bf16/int8) and keep it consistent across regions for the same model.

Regions + infrastructure
Regions: NA/EU/APAC where capacity is available.
- Example candidates: us-east, us-west, eu-west, eu-central, apac-sg (TBD final)

We must document:
- instance / accelerator family used per region (at least at a high level)
- any region-specific constraints (capacity or routing)

OPEN QUESTION: Do we keep hardware constant across regions (hard) or allow region-appropriate equivalents (likely)? If not identical, how do we explain without weakening the story?
Proposed language: “We reserved comparable high-performance GPU capacity in each region. Exact underlying hardware may vary by region; results reflect what Redwood customers can provision in-region during the measurement window.”

Runner + reproducibility
Harness
- benchmark-lab runner (Dockerized, pinned deps) executes region sweeps with a manifest.
- Each run produces:
  - run_manifest.json (inputs: model, region, workload, concurrency, runtime config)
  - raw per-request logs (redacted)
  - derived metrics tables

Manifest format
- Implemented in PR-4829.
- Required manifest fields (draft):
  - benchmark_version
  - runner_image_digest
  - model_id + model_version
  - region
  - workload_id
  - concurrency
  - warmup_requests
  - measurement_requests
  - start/end timestamps

Redaction
Public artifacts must exclude:
- request IDs that can be correlated with customer systems
- internal cluster IDs
- any API tokens
- full raw prompts
(see PR-4873 for redaction hooks; not yet incorporated in this doc)

Measurement protocol (draft)
Warmup
- Warmup phase: N_warmup requests per {model, region, workload, concurrency} to stabilize caches, kernel selection, and autoscaling.
- Warmup requests are excluded from published metrics.

OPEN QUESTION: What warmup size is sufficient across models? Candidates: 50 / 100 / 200 requests.

Measurement window
- After warmup, execute N_measure requests.
- Ensure stable offered load at target concurrency.

Concurrency model
We need to define what “concurrency = k” means.
Option A (closed-loop): maintain k in-flight requests; each client sends next request immediately after completion.
Option B (open-loop): Poisson arrivals tuned to a target QPS; concurrency emerges.

OPEN QUESTION: Which is more representative for our buyers?
- Closed-loop is easier to implement and reason about saturation; but may under-represent spiky production traffic.
- Open-loop is closer to real user traffic but harder to compare.

Current direction (engineering): closed-loop concurrency per PR-4829 runner.
We should include a note in the report that results reflect steady-state load at specified concurrency.

Caching / batching policy (sensitive)
This section is most likely to create confusion, so we need to be explicit.

What we need to specify
- Continuous batching: ON/OFF (and target batch limits)
- KV cache management strategy (default Redwood runtime)
- Prefix caching: ON/OFF and what constitutes a cache hit
- Any request-level caching (e.g., exact prompt cache): should be OFF for fairness unless the workload explicitly tests it

Current (likely) baseline policy (draft)
- Runtime continuous batching: ON (default Redwood runtime)
- Prefix caching: OFF for benchmark runs unless otherwise stated
- Request/result caching: OFF

OPEN QUESTION: Prefix caching is a real Redwood advantage for many production workloads, but enabling it in the benchmark makes comparisons harder and may be viewed as “optimizing for benchmark.”
Proposed compromise:
- Keep headline report with prefix caching OFF.
- Add an appendix section (“What happens with prefix caching enabled?”) with one workload slice + clear caveats.

Streaming
We need to decide whether to treat streaming responses differently.

OPEN QUESTION: Include streaming TTFT and “time to N tokens” metrics (e.g., time to 50 tokens) in public tables?
Pros: aligns with user-perceived responsiveness.
Cons: complexity; must ensure apples-to-apples across endpoints.

Current direction: publish TTFT and TPOT; keep streaming transport details consistent across runs; avoid “time to 50 tokens” unless we can standardize well.

Sampling parameters
We must fix sampling to avoid quality/length drift.
Draft defaults
- temperature = 0.2 (or 0.0 for deterministic?)
- top_p = 1.0
- max_output_tokens varies by workload (with an output distribution)
- stop sequences: workload-specific

OPEN QUESTION: temperature=0 is easiest for reproducibility but can change decoding behavior compared to real usage; temperature=0.2 is more realistic but can add output length variance.
Proposed: temperature=0.0 for benchmark stability + a note that this is for measurement determinism, not necessarily recommended for all apps.

Retries, errors, and exclusions
We need a clear policy.
Draft
- Count only successful 2xx responses.
- Track and report error rates separately (5xx, 429, timeouts).
- If error rate exceeds threshold (e.g., >0.5% during measurement), the run is invalid and must be rerun.
- For timeouts: exclude from latency distributions but include in “error rate” reporting.

OPEN QUESTION: Do we exclude “first request after scale-up” outliers? That can hide real cold-start behavior.
Proposed: do not exclude unless clearly identified as infrastructure failure; instead publish stability info and ensure warmup is adequate.

Stability gates / reruns
- Implemented in PR-4855.
- If p95 E2E varies more than X% across repeated runs, trigger auto-rerun.

Parameters (to finalize)
- repeats per cell: 3 (minimum)
- variance threshold: 7–10% (TBD)
- minimum samples: N_measure >= 500 requests (TBD based on runtime)

Aggregation across repeats
- Compute per-repeat metrics; then take median of repeats for published metric.
- Also publish “stability band” or note when variance was high.

OPEN QUESTION: Do we publish confidence intervals? Might be heavy for launch.
Proposed: publish variance notes and rerun policy; keep CI internal.

Normalization / fairness notes
We will include a “How to interpret this” section:
- Results depend on prompt length distribution, concurrency, and region capacity.
- Small changes in workload can change ranking.
- The benchmark is designed to reflect common production mixes, not worst-case or best-case for any single model.

Competitor baselines (if any)
This doc does not define competitor measurement; if we include competitor context, we must:
- Document endpoint type, region, and pricing assumptions
- Keep language caveated (“contextual baseline”, “as measured on date X”, “not a comprehensive comparison”)
- Retain raw substantiation artifacts per policy

Data retention
- Retain run manifests, raw redacted logs, and derived datasets used for public claims.
- Access controlled to Applied ML + Legal + PMM as needed.

TODO list (next 7 days)
1) Decide concurrency model (closed-loop vs open-loop) and write plain-English justification. (Claire + Rina)
2) Lock baseline caching policy for headline numbers; decide whether to include prefix caching appendix. (Jonas + Mateo + Soojin)
3) Finalize sampling params (temp/top_p/max tokens) and ensure output length distribution is controlled. (Claire)
4) Set warmup + measurement sample sizes; validate run time vs capacity reservations. (Rina + Vanessa)
5) Draft the “fairness + caveats” paragraph for Legal review. (Elliot + Soojin)
6) Add explicit definitions of latency/$ from PR-4821 into this doc verbatim (once finalized) to avoid drift. (Nadia)

Open questions (for methodology review meeting)
- Should the headline metric use p50 or p95 latency? If p50, how do we prevent buyers from thinking we are hiding tails?
- Should we publish results for multiple concurrencies or pick one “reference” concurrency (e.g., 16) and provide a slider on the web page?
- How do we handle different context windows across models for long-context tasks? Provide separate views or restrict to common window?
- Do we include Dedicated/Private numbers or keep to Hosted API only (and describe how Dedicated changes things)?

Notes / draft language candidates
Draft disclaimer language (needs Legal pass):
“Benchmarks are based on the described workloads and configurations, measured during a defined time window. Performance and cost can vary by region, model version, prompt characteristics, and traffic patterns. Results are intended to provide directional guidance for production inference economics rather than a guarantee for every workload.”

Draft “why latency/$” explanation:
“Tokens/sec is useful for understanding throughput, but product teams often optimize for user-perceived latency and infrastructure spend simultaneously. Latency/$ summarizes that tradeoff: lower is better, meaning you achieve a given responsiveness with less spend.”

Appendix ideas (optional)
- A1: Prefix caching ON vs OFF (one workload slice)
- A2: Concurrency sweep charts (k=1, 4, 16, 64)
- A3: Regional consistency: p95 heatmap + error rate bands

Changelog
- 2025-06-06: Initial skeleton created (Elliot)
- 2025-06-10: Added concurrency/caching open questions from methodology review (Claire/Jonas)
- 2025-06-19: Updated prompt set notes to v3; added stability gates references (Rina/Mei)
